hints: Start by reading the flat baseline at the left of each graph - what is the steady voltage before either action potential begins?
Now compare the vertical size of each spike from its own baseline up to the same peak of about $+40\text{ mV}$ - which cell starts higher so has less far to rise?
Look carefully at the time axes - Fig. 9.1 goes to $5\text{ ms}$ while Fig. 9.2 goes to $10\text{ ms}$ - measure how long depolarisation and the whole spike last in each.
Follow the trace just after repolarisation finishes - does one trace dip below its resting level while the other returns straight to baseline?
walkthrough:
Compare the Resting Baselines**
Both traces start flat, but at different voltages. In Fig. 9.1 the motor neurone sits at $-70\text{ mV}$, while in Fig. 9.2 the muscle fibre sits more negative at $-90\text{ mV}$. So the neurone resting potential is higher - less negative - than the muscle.

Compare the Size of the Spike**
Both reach the same peak of about $+40\text{ mV}$. Because the neurone starts higher, it changes less: $+40 - (-70) = 110\text{ mV}$ compared with $+40 - (-90) = 130\text{ mV}$ in muscle. Always state both values as a paired comparison with units.

Compare Speed and Shape**
The neurone spike is narrower and faster. Depolarisation takes about $1\text{ ms}$ in the neurone versus $2\text{ ms}$ in muscle, and the whole action potential lasts about $2.7\text{ ms}$ versus $4\text{ ms}$. After repolarisation the neurone dips to about $-90\text{ mV}$ - a hyperpolarisation - before returning to $-70\text{ mV}$, while the muscle returns directly to $-90\text{ mV}$ with no overshoot.

Final answer: Motor neurone has higher resting potential of $-70\text{ mV}$ vs $-90\text{ mV}$ in muscle; smaller depolarisation of $110\text{ mV}$ vs $130\text{ mV}$ in muscle; faster action potential of approx $2.7\text{ ms}$ vs $4\text{ ms}$ in muscle; motor neurone shows hyperpolarisation, muscle does not.

hints: In Fig. 9.3 tension stays flat for the first few ms after stimulation - if the muscle is not yet shortening, what electrical signal must first spread inside the fibre?
Think about where $Ca^{2+}$ is stored inside a muscle fibre and what happens to that store when the internal membranes depolarise.
Link that $Ca^{2+}$ release to the thin filament proteins - how does binding to one protein move another to uncover the myosin-binding sites on actin?
walkthrough:
Spread the Action Potential Inwards**
The latent phase is the delay between stimulation at $0\text{ ms}$ and tension rise at about $5\text{ ms}$. During this time the muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down the transverse T-tubules deep into the fibre. No sliding has started yet, which is why tension is flat.

Release Calcium Ions**
Depolarisation of the T-tubules triggers the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release its stored $Ca^{2+}$ by diffusion into the sarcoplasm surrounding the myofibrils. This rise in $Ca^{2+}$ is the chemical link between excitation and contraction.

Uncover Binding Sites and Form Cross-Bridges**
$Ca^{2+}$ binds to troponin on the thin filament. This changes troponin shape and pulls tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin. Myosin heads can then bind to actin to form cross-bridges, ready for the contraction phase when tension rises steeply.

Final answer: T-tubules depolarised; $Ca^{2+}$ diffuse out of sarcoplasmic reticulum; $Ca^{2+}$ bind to troponin causing tropomyosin to move and expose myosin-binding sites on actin so cross-bridges form.

hints: A whole muscle contains thousands of sarcomeres - do you think every myosin head lets go of actin at exactly the same instant?
walkthrough:
Not All Bridges Break Together**
Relaxation needs $Ca^{2+}$ pumping back and ATP to detach myosin. This does not happen synchronously in every sarcomere. Some fibres and sarcomeres are still attached and generating force while others have already let go, so overall tension declines smoothly over about $70\text{ ms}$ rather than dropping instantly.
Final answer: Myosin heads detach / cross-bridges break at different times, so tension falls gradually.
